sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content: Global equities were mixed as a multi-decade sovereign-bond sell-off dominated, before a softer US payrolls report lifted mega-cap tech into Friday's close. MSCI World rose roughly **0.7%** (approx., verify before merging), with MSCI Developed Markets similar and MSCI Emerging Markets broadly flat (approx., verify before merging). The S&P 500 slipped **0.3%** to **7,722.72** and the Dow fell **1.3%** to **51,176.96**, while the MAG7-led Nasdaq added **0.5%** to **27,190.86**. Europe lagged, with the Euro Stoxx 50 near **6,238** (approx., verify before merging) and the STOXX Europe 600 down about **1.1%** on the week. In APAC, the Nikkei 225 jumped **2.9%** to **68,309.46**, Hong Kong's Hang Seng slumped **5.2%** to **23,972.29**, and China's CSI 300 was shut for the Golden Week holiday.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equities finished mixed as a renewed bond-market rout overshadowed resilient growth, before a weak September jobs report sparked a late rally. The S&P 500 eased **0.3%** to **7,722.72** and the Dow dropped **1.3%** to **51,176.96**, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq rose **0.5%** to **27,190.86**, helped by a Friday advance of **0.7%** in the S&P 500 and **1.2%** in the Nasdaq.

The dominant force was surging yields: the 10-year UST climbed about **11bps** to **5.27%** and the 30-year rose **13bps** to **5.62%**, its highest since 2002, pressuring valuations as the S&P 500's earnings yield slipped roughly a percentage point below the 10-year. Hawkish Fed commentary and firm activity data early in the week stoked higher-for-longer fears.

Friday's softer-than-expected September payrolls proved the turning point, prompting traders to pare bets on an October Fed hike and triggering a tech-led bounce. Growth firmly outpaced value as mega-cap and AI-linked names led, while rate-sensitive, cyclical Dow constituents lagged over the week.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities fell on the week despite a Friday rebound, with the STOXX Europe 600 down roughly **1.1%** after touching a three-month low on Thursday; it then rallied **0.8%** on Friday. The Euro Stoxx 50 closed near **6,238** (approx., verify before merging), underperforming Wall Street.

The backdrop was dominated by a global bond sell-off and mounting French fiscal concerns, which drove sovereign yields higher before Friday's relief, when the German 10-year Bund fell over **6bps** to **3.454%**. Euro-area inflation accelerated more than expected in September to a three-year high, keeping the ECB hawkish, with markets pricing roughly **82%** odds of a December hike.

Dispersion was wide across sectors: banks suffered their biggest weekly fall since April on fears that higher rates would crimp growth, while technology names rebounded on renewed AI enthusiasm into the Friday close.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Japanese equities extended their run, with the Nikkei 225 rising **2.9%** for a third straight weekly gain to **68,309.46**, even after a modest **0.9%** dip on Friday. The yen stayed soft, with USD/JPY near **157.8**, after the BoJ's September summary of opinions offered fewer hawkish signals than investors had hoped.

Hong Kong told the opposite story: the Hang Seng tumbled **5.2%** to **23,972.29**, its worst week in over a year, as a renewed sell-off engulfed technology names. Mainland Chinese markets were closed for the Golden Week holiday, leaving the CSI 300 effectively unchanged on the week.

The regional split reflected the broader AI-versus-rates tug-of-war: soaring sovereign yields and stretched tech valuations sparked profit-taking across Asian growth names, even as Japanese banks and exporters benefited from higher yields and a weaker yen.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar broke higher as the global bond sell-off and safe-haven demand dominated, with the DXY briefly topping **102.00** to a fresh 2026 high. Firmer Fed tightening expectations early in the week underpinned the move, though softer Friday payrolls took some momentum out of the rally.

The euro bore the brunt, falling more than **1%** against both the dollar and Swiss franc as French fiscal concerns and politics weighed, with EUR/USD touching its lowest since May 2025. Sterling slid towards **1.3200**, near three-month lows and heading for a fifth consecutive weekly decline as surging global yields buoyed the dollar.

The yen also softened, with USD/JPY around **157.8**, after the BoJ meeting summary disappointed hawks. Rising developed-market yields pressured higher-beta and emerging-market currencies, extending the broad USD advance.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
The dominant theme was broad losses masking persistent supply risks, with the Bloomberg Commodity Index down **2.1%** as improving crude flows, harvest pressure and tighter financial conditions weighed on prices.

Crude traded lower as diplomatic progress eroded the geopolitical risk premium, with Saudi Arabia restoring exports through its East-West pipeline and US-Iran talks described as productive. Gold slipped within a downtrend from its August peak, pressured by higher real yields despite resilient ETF demand; it needs a break above **USD 4,235** to turn higher, while a drop below **USD 4,115** would put **USD 4,000** back in focus.

Copper retreated but held historically elevated levels, with net longs jumping **26%** to a 5½-year high of **82.6k** contracts on physical tightness and supply concerns. The pullback underscored how tighter financial conditions and surging yields are now pressing even supply-constrained markets.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
Sovereign bonds were at the centre of the week as a global sell-off drove yields to multi-decade highs. The 10-year UST rose about **11bps** to **5.27%** and the 30-year climbed **13bps** to **5.62%**, its highest since 2002, while the 1-year held near **4.45%**, steepening the curve.

Hawkish Fed commentary and signs of economic acceleration stoked higher-for-longer fears, compounded by French fiscal worries and a three-year high in euro-area inflation that lifted the German 10-year Bund towards **3.45%**. Friday's softer US payrolls brought relief, paring October hike bets and easing yields into the close.

With yields elevated, strategists flagged the eroding case for equities over bonds as the S&P 500's earnings yield fell roughly a percentage point below the 10-year. Credit tone stayed broadly resilient, however, with the late-week equity rebound keeping IG and HY sentiment steady despite the rate volatility.
